opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a bet on optionality and talent. If you look at the history of this field, a lot of the biggest value creation came from research breakthroughs that nobody could have turned into a product roadmap ahead of time. The transformer paper wasn't a product plan. Scaling laws weren't a product plan. But once those ideas existed, they unlocked enormous markets. So investors are essentially saying, "We think the next few of those breakthroughs are still out there, and the people most likely to find them are this particular group."

There's also a talent argument. The number of people who can really push the frontier, whether that's on architectures, on systems efficiency, or on training methods, is pretty small. If you can bring a concentrated group of those people together and give them compute and freedom, there's a decent chance something valuable comes out of it, even if you can't say exactly what. And the outcomes are very skewed. If one of these labs finds a way to make models ten times more efficient, or comes up with a fundamentally better architecture, that's worth a lot, either through licensing, through an acquisition, or eventually through building a product once the direction is clear.

From where I sit, having worked on things like FlashAttention and state space models, I've seen how research that looked kind of niche, just making attention faster on GPUs, turned out to matter a lot for the whole industry. So I'm sympathetic to the view that funding open-ended research can pay off.

That said, I'd be a bit cautious. Compute is expensive, and research without any feedback from real usage can drift. I think the healthiest setups have some connection to real workloads, so you know which problems actually matter. You don't need a product on day one, but you want to be grounded in what people will eventually need. So I'd describe it as a high-variance bet. Some of these efforts will look brilliant in hindsight and some won't, but given how much is still unknown in AI, I understand why people are making it.

r001.rationale: The response credits investors’ interest to the group’s talent and potential research breakthroughs, but does not mention Ilya or his personal reputation.

r002.rationale: It points to past research breakthroughs, including transformers and scaling laws, creating substantial value and unlocking markets, and frames investors’ current bets as a response to that track record.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it looks strange from the outside, but it actually makes a lot of sense once you accept one premise, which is that the model itself is the product. Or at least, the capability is the product. If you believe that the frontier of what these systems can do is still moving fast, then the thing that captures value isn't a nicely designed app on top, it's being the group that figures out the next step in how to train or run these models efficiently.

I've seen this from both sides, right, in academia and then at Together, and also just from knowing a lot of the people who've gone off to start these labs. The pitch isn't "we'll have a product in eighteen months." The pitch is more like, "here is a small set of people who have actually done the hard thing before, and if they do it again, the result is worth a lot, and there are many ways to monetize that later." Licensing, API access, getting acquired, becoming infrastructure for someone else. So the investors are kind of underwriting the research bet and deferring the product question, because historically the product question has turned out to be easier than the research question.

The other thing is that compute is the bottleneck, and that changes the economics. In a lot of fields, you could do foundational research in a university with a few GPUs. For training at the frontier you can't. So if you want to do that kind of work, you basically have to raise money like a startup even if you're organized more like a lab. Some of this is just research that needs venture-style funding because that's the only vehicle big enough.

Now, do I think all of these will work out? No. A lot of them will end up as very expensive papers. And I do think there's a dynamic where investors are partly buying talent and partly buying an option on something they can't fully evaluate, which is uncomfortable. But I'd push back on the idea that it's irrational. If you look at the things that actually mattered over the past few years, attention kernels, better inference, new architectures, mixture of experts, those came out of fairly research-shaped efforts, and the people who had them early got outsized returns. So the market is sort of correctly pricing that research progress has had unusually direct commercial consequences. Whether that stays true is the real question, and I think it depends on whether we keep finding big algorithmic wins or whether it all just becomes scale.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Ilya, SSI, or attribute investors’ funding decisions to anyone’s personal reputation.

r002.rationale: It says research advances such as attention kernels and new architectures brought outsized returns, so investors are pricing in research progress’ commercial consequences.

astra-6.text:
I think the bet is that if you have a team that can make a fundamental advance, there will be a way to capture value from that later. You might not know what the product is yet, but the research could create options—licensing the technology, partnering with another company, or eventually building something yourself.

The tension is that valuable research and a valuable business aren’t necessarily the same thing. You can do work that benefits the whole field without capturing much of that benefit. So I can understand funding research before there’s a product plan. But at some point, you still need an answer to why the value accrues to that company.

r001.rationale: The response describes investors betting on a team’s potential research advances, but does not attribute willingness to fund Ilya’s SSI venture to his personal reputation.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that AI risks are beginning to pay off or connect that to increased willingness to fund AI ventures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bet is that if you make a sufficiently important research breakthrough, you’ll have options for how to turn that into a business. You might not know what the product is today, but you’re betting that the capability will be valuable enough that you can figure that out later.

There’s a tension there, though. Research progress and capturing value from research are different things. You could do fantastic work that ends up benefiting the whole ecosystem without your company capturing much of that value. So I can understand funding a team before it has a product plan, but eventually there has to be some explanation for why the value accrues to that company. Otherwise, it’s closer to funding a research institute, which is valuable, but a different proposition.

r001.rationale: The response discusses funding research ventures generally but does not attribute willingness to fund Ilya’s SSI venture to his personal reputation.

r002.rationale: The response describes a bet on valuable research breakthroughs, but does not say investors are more willing to fund AI ventures because some AI risks are beginning to pay off.
